questions.explain: QUBO is short for Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization -- minimizing x^T Q x over binary vectors x, with no explicit constraint syntax.
f(1,1) = -5(1) + 2(1)(1) - 3(1) = -5 + 2 - 3 = -6, which is also the minimum across all four binary assignments.

questions.q: Why does a QUBO stay strictly quadratic (never needing cubic or higher terms) even though real cost functions can be complex?
options: Because for binary variables, x_i^2 = x_i, so diagonal terms collapse to linear terms and only pairwise cross terms x_i*x_j remain
Because QUBO only allows at most 2 variables total
Because quadratic terms are defined as equal to zero by convention
Because Q must always be a diagonal matrix
questions.explain: Since x_i is 0 or 1, x_i^2 equals x_i, which is why diagonal entries become plain linear terms and the only genuine interactions are the pairwise x_i*x_j cross terms -- this is also why QUBOs map cleanly onto hardware with two-body qubit interactions.

questions.q: How does a QUBO represent a real constraint like 'select exactly B of the variables,' given that QUBO has no native constraint syntax?
options: By adding a penalty term P*(sum of x_i - B)^2 to the objective, which is zero when the constraint holds and positive otherwise
By removing all variables that would violate the constraint from Q before solving
QUBO cannot represent constraints under any circumstances
By setting Q_ii to exactly B for every i
questions.explain: The standard pattern folds the constraint into the objective as a penalty term P*(sum x_i - B)^2, scaled large enough that constraint violation always costs more than any gain elsewhere in the objective.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does x = (1,1) still win even though Q_12 = +2 represents a penalty for selecting both items together?
options: Because the combined individual rewards (-5 and -3) outweigh the +2 interaction penalty, giving a net total of -6, still lower than any other assignment
Because penalties of +2 always dominate rewards of -5 and -3 regardless of sign
Because Q_12 = +2 actually represents a reward, not a penalty, in this convention
Because x1 and x2 cannot both equal 1 in a valid QUBO
questions.explain: f(1,1) = -5 + 2 - 3 = -6, which is still lower (better, since we're minimizing) than f(1,0) = -5 or f(0,1) = -3 -- the +2 penalty isn't strong enough to flip the decision, illustrating the trade-off a QUBO solver navigates.
